records.content: Tana Toraja (Toraja Land) is a highland region of South Sulawesi known for its dramatic funeral rites, boat-shaped tongkonan houses, and cliff-face gravesites. Traditional funerals are open to respectful visitors — bring cigarettes/candies as gifts for the family and dress modestly. Access via Makassar (UPG) then an 8-hour drive north to Rantepao. Culturally unique — very different from Bali or Java.

records.content: The Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary in Ubud is home to ~700 long-tailed macaques living around three ancient temples in a river gorge. Entry ~80k IDR foreigner. Rules: no plastic bags, no food, no eye contact with the alpha males, no fast movements. Toddlers should be carried — the monkeys can be aggressive.

Sardjito Hospital is the largest public teaching hospital. For minor traveller ailments, private clinics on Jalan Malioboro or in Prawirotaman are cheaper.

records.content: Pura Luhur Uluwatu sits on a 70-metre cliff on the southern tip of Bali — one of the six major sea temples. The daily Kecak fire dance at sunset (starts around 18:00, book ahead) is a compact retelling of the Ramayana with chanting and fire. Watch out for macaque monkeys who steal sunglasses and phones — remove and pocket everything before entering.

records.content: Nusa Lembongan is Nusa Penida's smaller, gentler neighbour — 30 minutes from Sanur by fast-boat. Highlights: Devil's Tear (dramatic waves and blowholes), Dream Beach, mangrove tours, and the yellow suspension bridge to Nusa Ceningan. Much slower pace than Bali; good for a 2–3 night couple's / family stopover.

records.content: Lake Toba (Danau Toba) is the world's largest volcanic lake, formed by a supervolcanic eruption ~74,000 years ago. Samosir Island in the middle is the traditional home of the Batak people and the base for most travellers. Fly into Kualanamu (Medan · KNO) or Silangit (DTB · closer). Peaceful, cool, few crowds — a great non-Bali Indonesia experience.
questions: How do I visit Lake Toba?
What is there to see at Lake Toba?

records.content: The Derawan Islands (Kepulauan Derawan) in East Kalimantan are famous for stingless jellyfish lake on Kakaban, manta rays at Sangalaki, whale sharks at Talisayan, and green turtles nesting on Derawan. Access via Berau (BEJ) then a 2-hour speedboat. Remote, quiet, few international tourists. Best May–October.

records.content: Bunaken Marine Park, off Manado (MDC), is one of Indonesia's premier diving destinations. Wall dives with reef sharks, turtles, and pelagics. Best season April–November (calm seas). Base yourself at Bunaken Island itself or on Manado Tua/Siladen for shorter boat rides. Combine with Lembeh Strait (muck diving, macro photography) on the same trip.
questions: What is there to see at Bunaken?

records.content: For lost passport, serious legal trouble, or a fatality abroad, contact your country's embassy or consulate in Jakarta (most main embassies) or the consular office in Denpasar (Bali) — Australia, UK, and USA all maintain consular presence in Bali. Save the 24-hour emergency line before travel. Embassies do NOT pay medical bills or repatriate — that's your travel insurance's job.

records.content: Tanah Lot is a Hindu temple on a small rocky islet off Bali's west coast, ~30 km from Denpasar. Access is only possible at low tide across a rock causeway — the temple itself is off-limits to non-worshippers. Sunset is the classic time to visit but it gets very crowded; arrive 90 minutes before sunset for a good photo spot. Small entry fee (~75k IDR foreigner).

records.content: Nusa Penida is a rugged island south-east of Bali, a 30-minute fast-boat from Sanur. Highlights: Kelingking Beach (the famous T-Rex-shaped cliff), Angel's Billabong, Broken Beach, Diamond Beach, Crystal Bay for snorkelling with manta rays. Roads are steep and narrow — hire a local driver rather than a scooter unless experienced. Day trip is possible but rushed; 2 nights is better.

records.content: Tegalalang Rice Terraces, ~15 minutes north of Ubud, are Bali's most-photographed rice fields — cascading levels carved into a valley. Free entry to the walking path, though local farmers ask for a small 'donation' (10–20k IDR is fair). The famous Bali swings and 'love nest' installations add to the crowds. Go before 9 AM to avoid tour buses.

records.content: The Dayak Iban are one of many Dayak subgroups spread across Kalimantan (Borneo). Traditional longhouse (rumah betang / rumah panjai) communities on major rivers. Aluk Todolo-like animist beliefs coexist with Christianity, with adat law regulating land, marriage, and dispute. Visiting a longhouse: approach through the tuai rumah (headman), remove shoes, accept offered tuak (rice wine) with the right hand (a small sip is respectful — full refusal can be rude).

records.content: The Baduy (Kanekes) are a Sundanese adat community in western Java, ~11,000 people. Divided into Baduy Dalam (Inner Baduy, ~1,200, strict adherence — no electricity, motorised transport, cameras, soap, or synthetic cloth) and Baduy Luar (Outer Baduy, more flexible). Visitors may enter Baduy Luar with a local guide; Baduy Dalam entry requires the guide's introduction and strict rule observance (no photos of people, no ATM/mobile use during the visit, respect for pikukuh customary law). Access: Ciboleger village, ~4 hours from Jakarta.
questions: What are the rules for Baduy?

records.content: The Mentawai people live on the Mentawai Islands off West Sumatra's coast — culturally + linguistically distinct from mainland Minangkabau. Known for sikerei (shamans), extensive body tattooing (titi), sharpened teeth traditions (increasingly rare), and Arat Sabulungan animist religion (now a recognised penghayat kepercayaan). Deep-interior visits (Siberut) require multi-day trekking + local guide; respectful visits arranged through community-based tourism operators.
questions: What are the rules for Mentawai?

records.content: Sade village (Rembitan, central Lombok) is a Sasak adat village widely opened to respectful tourism — thatched-roof lumbung (rice barn) houses, weaving demonstrations, and preserved marriage-by-elopement (kawin lari) tradition. Entry: donation to the community box (~30k IDR fair). Local guides offered — negotiate before starting. Do not enter houses uninvited. The nearby Ende village is a quieter alternative less on the tour circuit.

records.content: The Toraja are a highland South Sulawesi adat community (~1M people) organised around Aluk Todolo (their pre-Christian religion — now a recognised penghayat kepercayaan) alongside Protestant Christianity. Most famous for rambu solo' (elaborate multi-day funeral rites) and tongkonan (boat-shaped ancestral houses). Visitors are welcome at funerals as respectful guests; customary gifts (cigarettes, sugar, palm wine) are appropriate. Do not photograph without asking; wear dark colours; expect emotional intensity.
questions: What are the rules for Toraja?

records.content: Galungan celebrates the victory of dharma (good) over adharma (evil) — the Balinese Hindu equivalent of a major religious holiday, observed every 210 days on the Pawukon calendar. Homes and shops erect penjor (tall curved bamboo poles decorated with palm-leaf ornaments) along the streets. Many Balinese travel to their family home; expect quieter tourist zones but busier villages. Ends 10 days later with Kuningan. Most businesses stay open in tourist areas, but staff numbers thin — book restaurants ahead.
questions: What are the rules for Galungan?

records.content: Cap Go Meh marks the 15th day (final day) of Chinese New Year celebrations, most vividly in Indonesia's Chinese-Indonesian communities — Singkawang (West Kalimantan) hosts arguably the largest, with tatung (spirit-medium) processions that draw international visitors. Also strong in Jakarta's Glodok, Semarang, Surabaya, Bogor, and Pontianak. Not a national public holiday but the underlying Imlek (Chinese New Year) is.

records.content: Kuningan marks the end of the 10-day Galungan period on the Balinese Pawukon calendar. Ancestral spirits, believed to have visited the earthly realm during Galungan, return to the heavens at noon on Kuningan — so ceremonies traditionally end by midday. Yellow rice (nasi kuning) is the ceremonial food. Best time for visitors to observe: a village temple ceremony in the morning; ask permission before entering.
questions: What are the rules for Kuningan?

records.content: Idul Fitri (Lebaran, Eid al-Fitr) marks the end of Ramadan — Indonesia's biggest annual holiday. The two official public holidays surround a national exodus (mudik) as millions travel to their family village. Transport prices spike 2–3× for the week either side; airports, trains, ferries fully booked. Jakarta becomes eerily quiet; tourist areas continue normally. Halal bi halal (mutual forgiveness visits) fill the days after. Book any long-distance travel 2 months ahead of Lebaran week.

How should tourists handle Idul Fitri?
Is Idul Fitri important in Indonesia?

records.content: Ramadan is the Islamic month of fasting — Muslims abstain from food, drink, and smoking from fajr (pre-dawn) to maghrib (sunset). In Indonesia (world's largest Muslim country) many warungs close during daylight or draw a curtain across the front; some fully close for the month. Business hours shift; expect reduced service. After sunset, buka puasa (breaking of the fast) begins — bazaars pop up nationwide selling takjil (sweet snacks) + iftar meals. Non-Muslims are welcome to eat at hotels and non-halal restaurants; being discreet in public during daylight is a courtesy. Runs a lunar month (varies annually).
questions: What are the rules for Ramadan?

records.content: Melasti is a Balinese purification ceremony held 3–4 days before Nyepi. Villages carry sacred temple objects (pratima) in procession to the sea or a holy spring for symbolic cleansing. Coastal beaches (Sanur, Kuta, Padang Padang) fill with white-clad worshippers. Non-Hindu visitors may respectfully observe from a distance; do not photograph individual worshippers without permission and do not walk between the procession and the sea.
questions: What are the rules for Melasti?

records.content: Erau is the annual cultural festival of the Kutai Kartanegara sultanate in Tenggarong, East Kalimantan — traditionally centred on the enthronement anniversary. Modern Erau (revived in the 1970s) runs about a week and includes Dayak dance, boat races on the Mahakam river, tepong tawar (blessing rituals), and the belimbur (mutual water-throwing) finale. Typically held in September or October.
questions: What are the rules for Erau?

records.content: Nyepi is Bali's Day of Silence — the Balinese Hindu new year according to the Saka calendar. For 24 hours (roughly 06:00 to 06:00 next day) the entire island observes silence: no travel, no lights, no fires, no work, no entertainment. The airport (DPS) closes to arrivals + departures. Tourists must stay inside their hotel compound; only emergency vehicles operate. The night before is Pengrupukan, when huge papier-mâché ogoh-ogoh monsters are paraded and burned. Falls in March (varies annually · Saka calendar).
questions: What are the rules for Nyepi?

records.content: Odalan is a Balinese temple anniversary — every temple celebrates one every 210 days (Pawukon) or 355 days (lunar), meaning multiple happen every day across Bali. The temple is filled with offerings, gamelan music, and dance performances. Visitors are welcome if respectful: sarong + sash required, do not walk in front of praying worshippers, do not sit higher than the priests, no menstruating women per Balinese Hindu convention. Ask a local or your accommodation whether a nearby odalan is happening.
questions: What are the rules for Odalan?

records.content: Bau Nyale is an annual Sasak festival on Lombok's south coast (around Kuta Lombok) — thousands gather at night to catch nyale, a sea worm that surfaces once a year in February or March according to the traditional calendar. The worms are considered incarnations of the legendary Princess Mandalika. The event is preceded by a night of song, poetry (bepantun), and cultural performance. A significant recent-revival tradition tied to Sasak identity.

records.content: Waisak (Vesak) is the Buddhist commemoration of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death — celebrated on the full moon of the lunar month of Vesakha (usually May). In Indonesia the largest observance is at Borobudur: thousands of monks and pilgrims gather, meditate, and release lanterns into the night sky. The lantern release is ticketed; access to the temple upper terraces is highly restricted that day. Book lantern tickets months ahead. Public holiday nationally.
questions: What are the rules for Waisak?

records.content: Idul Adha (Eid al-Adha) is the Islamic 'Feast of Sacrifice', ~70 days after Idul Fitri. Sheep, goats, and cows are ritually sacrificed at mosques nationwide; meat is distributed to the poor. Public holiday. Less travel disruption than Idul Fitri but expect some restaurant menu changes (more mutton, goat curry). Non-Muslims visiting a mosque during the ceremony should ask permission and dress modestly.

records.content: Mie goreng is Indonesian fried noodles — yellow egg noodles stir-fried with kecap manis (sweet soy), garlic, shallots, chilli, cabbage, and often chicken, prawn or egg. The instant version (Indomie Mi Goreng) is a cultural phenomenon in its own right and available worldwide. The warung version at 15–25k IDR is a filling, cheap comfort meal.
questions: Where can I try Mie Goreng?

records.content: Nasi campur (literally 'mixed rice') is a plate of rice with a small selection of side dishes chosen by the customer — typical items include tempeh, tofu, egg, sambal, sayur (vegetables), chicken, and fish. Each region has its own style: Balinese nasi campur is often served with satay lilit and lawar, while Chinese-Indonesian nasi campur includes char siu and braised pork. A cheap, honest lunch (25–50k IDR).
questions: Where can I try Nasi Campur?

records.content: Es teler is a classic Indonesian dessert drink — shredded ice, jackfruit, young coconut, avocado, condensed milk, and pandan syrup. Cooling, filling, and cheap (15–25k IDR at a warung). Sister dessert es campur (mixed ice) adds cendol (green rice-flour jelly) and grass jelly. Great after a spicy meal on a hot afternoon.
questions: Where can I try es Teler?

records.content: Nasi Padang is the classic Padang-style presentation from West Sumatra: rice served with 10–15 small dishes brought to your table — rendang, gulai ayam (chicken curry), sambal ijo (green chilli), telur balado (spicy egg), sayur nangka (jackfruit curry) — and you pay only for what you eat. Rumah Makan Padang (Padang restaurants) are everywhere in Indonesia. Very spicy by default; ask for 'tidak pedas' if you want mild.
questions: Where can I try Nasi Padang?

records.content: Gado-gado is Indonesia's warm salad — steamed vegetables (long beans, cabbage, bean sprouts, potato, boiled egg, tofu, tempeh) topped with a spiced peanut sauce and prawn crackers. Naturally vegetarian if you skip the shrimp paste (terasi) in the sauce — ask 'tanpa terasi' for a fully vegan version. Excellent light lunch, especially in Jakarta and West Java.
questions: Where can I try Gado Gado?

records.content: Bakmi is Indonesian-Chinese egg noodles served either dry (bakmi ayam — with braised chicken, greens, and fried shallots) or in soup (bakmi kuah). Popular chains: Bakmi GM, Bakmi Naga, Bakmi Aloi. Almost always served with a side bowl of clear broth and sambal. A good option when you want something less spicy than most Indonesian food.

Ayam bakar is Indonesian grilled chicken — marinated in kecap manis, garlic, tamarind, and turmeric, then finished over charcoal. Sold with rice, sambal, lalapan (raw leaves), and a small dish of soup broth. Regional variants: ayam bakar Taliwang (Lombok, super-spicy chilli glaze), ayam bakar Wong Solo (Central Java, sweeter). 30–50k IDR at a warung.
questions: Where can I try Ayam Bakar?

records.content: Martabak comes in two very different forms. Martabak manis (sweet martabak, also called terang bulan) is a thick pancake stuffed with chocolate, cheese, condensed milk, peanuts, or Nutella — the classic Indonesian night snack. Martabak telur (savoury) is a thin dough wrap filled with minced meat, egg, and spring onion, pan-fried and served with pickles and curry sauce. Sold at street carts in every city, especially busy after 7 PM.

Babi guling is Balinese spit-roasted suckling pig, seasoned with a paste of turmeric, coriander, chilli, lemongrass, galangal, and shrimp paste. Served with rice, lawar (spiced vegetable-and-coconut mix), and crackling. Most famous at Ibu Oka in Ubud, Warung Babi Guling Pak Malen in Seminyak, and countless village stalls. Not halal — served openly in Bali because of the Hindu population.
questions: Where can I try Babi Guling?

records.content: Pura Besakih (the 'Mother Temple') is Bali's largest and holiest Hindu temple complex — 23 separate temples on the slopes of Mount Agung. Belief tradition: Balinese Hindu (Agama Hindu Dharma). Observance type: doctrinal + traditional. Access rules: sarong + sash mandatory (rental available), no entry to inner sanctuaries during ceremonies except for worshippers, no menstruating women per Balinese Hindu convention, tourist entry via a paved path with local-guide encouragement (agree fee first — 100–200k IDR is fair). Entry fee ~60k IDR foreigner.
questions: What are the rules for Besakih?

records.content: Masjid Istiqlal is South-East Asia's largest mosque — Jakarta's national mosque, capacity 200,000+. Belief tradition: Sunni Islam. Observance type: doctrinal. Notably located directly across from the Catholic Jakarta Cathedral — a symbol of Indonesian religious pluralism. Non-Muslim visitors are welcome outside of prayer times; dress modestly (shoulders + knees covered, headscarf provided for women at the entrance). Free entry; a guide-tip is customary. Do not photograph worshippers mid-prayer.
questions: What are the rules for Istiqlal?

records.content: Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist temple (9th-century Sailendra dynasty) — a functioning Buddhist site as well as a UNESCO monument. Belief tradition: Theravada + Mahayana Buddhist. Observance type: doctrinal + tourist-facing. Timed entry to upper terraces (foreigner ~US$25–35) since 2022; sunrise access ticketed separately. Local Buddhist community observes Waisak here in May — access restricted that day. Visitors dress modestly, walk clockwise around the stupas, do not touch reliefs.
questions: What are the rules for Borobudur?

records.content: Prambanan is a 9th-century Hindu temple complex — the largest in Indonesia — dedicated to the Trimurti (Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva). Belief tradition: Historical + revived Hindu practice (mostly Balinese Hindus visit for observances). Observance type: doctrinal (revived) + tourist-facing. UNESCO listed. Sarong + sash required for the main temples (rental included with ticket). Combine-ticket with Borobudur available. Dry-season Ramayana ballet in the outdoor amphitheatre most weekends — book ahead.
questions: What are the rules for Prambanan?

records.content: Pura Tirta Empul (in Tampaksiring, near Ubud) is the temple of holy spring water — a working Hindu pilgrimage site where Balinese come for melukat (purification bathing) at 30-plus spouts. Belief tradition: Balinese Hindu, active use. Observance type: doctrinal + contemporary practice. Visitors may bathe respectfully: change into a sarong + shorts in the changing area, do not use the two spouts reserved for funeral cleansing (marked; ask staff), do not photograph individuals mid-prayer, women should not enter the pools during menstruation.

Macaque monkeys will snatch sunglasses, phones, hats — bag them before entering. The daily Kecak fire dance at sunset (starts ~18:00) is a cultural performance held in a nearby amphitheatre — not part of the temple ritual itself.
